Business plan text:

Permitpath
Executive Summary: Permitpath
Problem
Small contractors lose a surprising amount of time and money to building permits. A typical
remodeling or trade firm has between two and twenty employees, and the owner usually does the
paperwork at night after a full day on site. Each city has its own application forms, its own
online portal and its own checklist of required attachments, and many of the rules are not
written down anywhere. A contractor who works in three or four cities has to learn three or
four different systems.
The cost of getting it wrong is high. When an application is rejected, it goes back into the
queue, and a correction can add one to four weeks. During that time crews sit idle, materials
are stored, and customers become unhappy. In interviews with 41 contractors over the last year,
34 told us they had lost at least one job start date in the past six months because of a permit
problem. Most said they track their open permits in a notebook, a spreadsheet or their email
inbox, and several admitted they had missed a reviewer's request for changes because the notice
went to a spam folder.
Solution
Permitpath is a desktop application that sits between the contractor and the city systems. The
contractor enters a job once: the address, the scope of work, the licenses and insurance
details, and the drawings. Permitpath then prepares the application for the chosen city,
filling in the fields and flagging anything missing. Before submission it runs the application
against a checklist built from that city's published requirements and from the reasons for
rejection that our users have reported to us. After submission it tracks the status and sends
reminders when a reviewer comments or a deadline is near.
The main difference from other tools is that Permitpath works across cities. Most existing
products are built for one city or are sold to the city itself. We are built for the
contractor, who is the person who actually feels the pain. We chose a desktop application
because many of our users work with large drawing files and prefer to keep their client data on
their own machines, and because it lets us work with several city portals without depending on
any one of them to give us access.
Market
The United States has roughly 700,000 small construction firms with fewer than twenty
employees. We focus first on residential remodelers and the electrical, plumbing and mechanical
trades, which file the most permits relative to their size. If even one in ten of these firms
paid us the price of our standard license, the market would be worth well over 100 million
dollars a year. We do not need all of those firms. Our plan targets the 25 largest metropolitan
areas, where contractors often cross city lines in a single week, and our first goal is 1,500
paying firms.
Business Model
Permitpath is sold as an annual license. Our standard plan costs 780 dollars per year for one
user and up to five cities, and our team plan costs 1,800 dollars per year for up to five users
and unlimited cities. We add new cities as paid expansions of a license only when a customer
asks for one that is not yet supported. Our cost to serve a customer is low: the software runs
on the customer's computer, and our main costs are the engineers who maintain the city
connections and a small support team. We expect gross margin above 80 percent once we reach
scale. We also plan a later add-on for suppliers and insurers, who want reliable data on permit
status, but we are not relying on it in our forecast.
Competition

Our competitors fall into three groups. The first is general project management software for
contractors, which is broad but does not know anything about the rules of a specific city. The
second is the permit portals that cities operate, which are the system of record but are
designed for the city's staff and not for the applicant. The third is permit expediting
services, where a person is hired to file and follow up on applications. These services work
well but cost several hundred dollars per application, which is too much for a small firm with
many jobs. Permitpath offers some of the same benefit at a small fraction of the price. We
think our strongest protection is the growing set of city-specific rules and rejection patterns
that our software learns from its users, which would take a new entrant a long time to rebuild.
Team
Dana Okonkwo-Reyes, chief executive, studies business administration at our university. Before
starting the company she spent three summers working for her uncle's remodeling firm, where she
handled permits and first saw the problem. Marcus Veltrane, chief technology officer, is a
computer science student who built the first prototype and leads our engineering. Priya
Anandakrishnan, head of customer development, studies urban planning and previously interned in
a city permitting office, which gives us a rare view of how reviewers actually read
applications. We are advised by a retired building official and by a small business lawyer who
has helped us with our contracts.
Milestones and Financials
Over the past year we defined the concept, built a working prototype and tested it with 12
pilot contractors in four cities. In the pilot, first-review rejections fell from about 38
percent of applications to about 14 percent, and the average time to approval fell by roughly
nine days. Eight of the twelve pilot firms converted to paid annual licenses, and we now have
23 paying customers and about 19,000 dollars in annual recurring revenue. We have registered
the company and launched a website that has produced most of our recent leads. We have also
raised 60,000 dollars from a small group of angel investors and a regional startup grant, which
we are using for development and for a part-time support hire. Our forecast is 120 customers
and 95,000 dollars in recurring revenue by the end of next year, and 600 customers and about
470,000 dollars by the end of the year after. We expect to reach break-even at about 450
customers.
What We Ask For
We are applying for the competition's prize money and for mentoring. We would use a prize of
25,000 dollars to add support for eight more cities, which is the most common request from our
waiting list, and to hire a second engineer for the summer. Beyond the money, we would value
introductions to contractor associations and to local governments, since both groups influence
which tools small firms trust. We would also welcome advice from experienced founders on
pricing and on when to move from a desktop product to a hybrid product that includes a web
component.

Question: Comment on the viability and scalability of the business model and strategy. Address whether the company has a clear path to making money and growing, and evaluate the validity of the entrepreneur's assumptions.

response.text:
The business model and strategy of Permitpath show reasonable viability and scalability, but key assumptions require closer scrutiny.

**Viability and Scalability:**
- **Revenue Model:** The annual licensing model is straightforward and aligns with the recurring revenue needs of small contractors. The pricing is positioned as a cost-effective alternative to permit expediting services, which is a valid differentiator.
- **Scalability:** The model is scalable in theory, as the software can be expanded to more cities and users without significant incremental costs. The desktop application reduces dependency on city portals, which enhances flexibility and reduces integration complexity.
- **Market Potential:** The target market (700,000 small firms) is substantial, and the focus on high-traffic areas (25 largest metros) is strategic. The $100M+ annual revenue potential is plausible if the company captures even a small percentage of the target market.

**Path to Making Money:**
- The company has already achieved some traction with 23 paying customers and $19,000 in ARR. The projected growth to 120 customers and $95,000 ARR by the end of next year is achievable with continued product development and marketing.
- The gross margin above 80% at scale is a strong indicator of financial health, assuming the cost structure remains stable.

**Assumptions and Validity:**
- **City-Specific Rules and Rejection Patterns:** The claim that Permitpath's learning from user data creates a competitive moat is valid, but the time and resources required to build this dataset must be validated. A new entrant could replicate this with sufficient data and time.
- **User Adoption and Retention:** The assumption that contractors will switch from spreadsheets or notebooks to a paid software solution is reasonable, but the current conversion rate (8 of 12 pilots) is modest. The company must demonstrate stronger retention and upsell potential.
- **Market Penetration:** The assumption that one in ten of the targeted firms will pay the standard license is optimistic. The company may need to validate this with more data or adjust pricing and value propositions.
- **Competitive Differentiation:** While Permitpath differentiates itself by focusing on the contractor rather than the city, the threat of competitors (especially permit expediting services) remains, especially if the pricing is not clearly superior.

**Conclusion:**
Permitpath has a viable and scalable business model, with a clear path to profitability. However, the company must validate key assumptions about market penetration, user adoption, and the uniqueness of its data-driven approach. The current traction is a positive sign, but the business will need to demonstrate consistent growth and strong customer retention to achieve long-term scalability.
